chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
title: B. C. Canard and the Four Tons of Rhythm
summary: They praise altoist B. C. Canard, his brother Ben's audition for Hampton, and the Four Tons of Rhythm in Chicago.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Well, we've got to go over some of those records you made out on the Coast. Well, Herman and Woody Walker, Woody is pretty much -- he's left the business hasn't he?
Yeah, he left I'd say 20 years ago.

All the work I can get, Herman is right there with me. I can't seem to get enough to please him. Oh, one of the really, great, great alto players who probably is not so well known outside of Kansas City but whom we have listened to and played with and who passed in 1967, one of the greatest I've ever heard is B.C. Canard. What would you
like to say about B.C. Canard? B.C. Canard was one of the greatest I've heard in many years and you don't hear that -- with the tone and everything and --
Didn't he go -- as I remember, you know Ben, who's been with me for 12 years, his brother, younger brother --
-- as I understand it, Hampton was in town and wanted B.C. to audition for him for his band and B was with somebody else. Who was B with -- and he sent his kid brother.
Four Tons of Rhythm -- and he sent Ben over for the audition and Ben wound up playing for Hampton for seven years.
Now, did B ever play with Hines?
See, he went to Chicago and played with the -- the Four Tons were in Chicago about three or four years; Clint Weaver and Jim Daddy Walker --
-- great guitar man and Clint Weaver on bass --
Oh Pop C, may God rest his soul.
-- and I named B.C. didn't I?
Well, there were four of them; Jim Daddy, B.C. -- and the boy out in Omaha, what was his name?
